# Pattern Catalog: Postgres-Backed Desired-State Reconciler in Rust for a microVM Fleet

Confidence labels: items are VERIFIED against the cited primary/secondary source unless marked UNVERIFIED.

## Section 1 - kube-rs controller-runtime loop shape

P1. Reconcile-the-object, never the event
- Mechanism: reconciler signature is reconcile(obj, ctx) -> Result<Action, Error>; the trigger reason is deliberately hidden. kube-rs: "This mapping mechanism ultimately hides the reason for the reconciliation request, and forces you to write an idempotent reconciler."
- Who: kube-rs kube_runtime::Controller, Go controller-runtime.
- Copy: reconciler input = (worktree_id) only. It re-reads the binding row + lease row + live VM state from the CH adapter every pass, and computes actions from the diff. Never pass "vm_crashed" or "lease_expired" event payloads into the reconciler.
- Avoid: event-payload-driven handlers ("on crash do X") - they break on missed/duplicated events.
- Sources: https://kube.rs/controllers/reconciler/ , https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/runtime/struct.Controller.html

P2. Check-every-property idempotency
- Mechanism: kube.rs guide: "assume nothing about why reconciliation started; assume the reconciler could have failed at any question mark; check every property independently" - independent "if missing { create }" checks, not sequential scripts.
- Who: kube-rs guide (normative requirement: "A reconciler must be idempotent").
- Copy: directly. Each pass: does VM process exist? does snapshot manifest match? is lease fresh? - each check independently repairable.
- Avoid: multi-step "workflows" where step 3 assumes step 2's in-memory result survived a crash.
- Source: https://kube.rs/controllers/reconciler/

P3. Action::requeue(Duration) / Action::await_change + separate error_policy
- Mechanism: reconciler returns a scheduling decision; errors route to a separate error_policy(obj, err, ctx) -> Action callback that owns backoff.
- Who: kube-rs.
- Copy: same return type for the Postgres reconciler - success returns Requeue(interval) or AwaitChange; errors go through one central policy that computes backoff and records the failure in EventLedger.
- Avoid: ad-hoc tokio::time::sleep retries inside the reconcile body.
- Source: https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/runtime/struct.Controller.html

P4. Finalizer split: Apply vs Cleanup, cleanup-before-delete guarantee
- Mechanism: kube-rs finalizer() helper: "if Event::Apply is ever started then Event::Cleanup must succeed before the Kubernetes object deletion completes"; both "must be idempotent, and tolerate being executed several times (even if previously cancelled)"; cleanup must "tolerate Event::Apply never having ran at all."
- Who: kube-rs runtime finalizer module.
- Copy: model as a Postgres column, not K8s metadata: binding rows get deleted_at_utc (tombstone) instead of DELETE. Reconciler sees tombstone -> runs teardown (kill VM, delete snapshot dirs, release lease) -> only then hard-deletes or archives the row. Teardown must tolerate a binding whose VM was never actually created.
- Avoid: copying K8s finalizer metadata machinery; also note the documented failure mode "object deletes will get stuck while the controller is not running" - surface stuck tombstones as an alert.
- Source: https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/runtime/finalizer/fn.finalizer.html

P5. What only makes sense with K8s API machinery (skip list)
- Skip: reflectors/watch caches (Postgres IS the store; no cache-coherency layer needed), owner-reference traversal (owns()/watches()), server-side apply, admission webhooks, the etcd resourceVersion optimistic-concurrency dance (generation fencing already covers this), and client-go-style shared informers.
- Copy from the same layer instead: the scheduler/dedup queue idea - pending triggers for the same worktree collapse to one queued reconcile.
- Sources: https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/runtime/struct.Controller.html , https://deepwiki.com/kube-rs/kube/4.2-controllers-and-reconciliation

## Section 2 - Level-triggered vs edge-triggered

P6. Level-triggered core, edge-triggered wake-up
- Mechanism: K8s controllers are "implemented on top of event streams, but their reconciliation logic is level-based... The trigger is event-driven; the behavior is not." Missed event => next reconciliation catches it anyway; edge-triggered => missed event = missed action, permanently.
- Who: all K8s controllers; explicitly discussed in kube-rs docs and K8s community writing.
- Copy: exactly this split. Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY (or EventLedger append) is only the wake-up hint; the reconciler always recomputes from full current rows.
- Avoid: treating a NOTIFY payload as the work item.
- Sources: https://medium.com/hackernoon/level-triggering-and-reconciliation-in-kubernetes-1f17fe30333d , https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/the-principle-of-reconciliation , https://kube.rs/controllers/reconciler/

P7. LISTEN/NOTIFY is a hint, not a queue
- Mechanism: Postgres notifications are ephemeral - "nothing is stored for a listener that is disconnected"; no replay; NOTIFY-carrying commits serialize on a global lock; breaks behind transaction-mode PgBouncer. Field pattern: jobs live in a table claimed via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; NOTIFY only wakes idle workers early.
- Who: standard Postgres practice; documented in official docs + queue guides.
- Copy: reconciler wakes on (a) NOTIFY from binding/lease writes, (b) a periodic tick. Both paths run the identical full read-and-diff.
- Avoid: relying on NOTIFY delivery for correctness; putting payloads in NOTIFY that the reconciler acts on directly.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-notify.html , https://nerdleveltech.com/postgres-listen-notify-job-queue

P8. Periodic requeue-everything as drift correction
- Mechanism: kube-rs .reconcile_all_on() re-triggers all managed objects; Oxide RPWs combine "periodic activation" (fixed intervals, "providing automatic repair of any missed updates") with "explicit activation."
- Who: kube-rs, Oxide Omicron/Nexus.
- Copy: full-fleet resync tick (e.g. every 60-300s) that enqueues every non-tombstoned binding. This is also the ongoing version of boot-time orphan reconciliation - orphan detection stops being a boot-only special case.
- Avoid: making the resync interval so short it masks bugs in the event path; log which path (tick vs notify) triggered each pass so drift-caught-by-tick is visible in EventLedger.
- Sources: https://docs.rs/kube/latest/kube/runtime/struct.Controller.html , https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373

P9. Oxide RPW watch-channel activation collapse
- Mechanism: RFD 373: activation via a tokio watch channel - "multiple activation signals collapse into one, since RPWs only need to know IF they've been activated, not how many times."
- Who: Oxide Nexus background tasks (production Rust control plane over CockroachDB - the closest field analog to Handshake's design).
- Copy: per-reconciler tokio::sync::watch (or Notify) as the dedup'd wake signal fed by both LISTEN and the tick.
- Avoid: unbounded mpsc queues of triggers - RFD 373 explicitly warns "large queues can stress database and protocol limits and trigger request/query timeouts" and cause thundering herds on recovery.
- Source: https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373

## Section 3 - microVM fleet managers in the field

P10. Flintlock plan/step reconciliation
- Mechanism: each microVM has spec + status + version; a reconcile loop chooses a Create/Update/Delete PLAN, where a plan is an ordered list of idempotent steps executed against the host (ADR 0004 merged create/update into one plan). Backed by containerd for image/snapshot state.
- Who: liquidmetal-dev/flintlock (Go; Firecracker + experimental Cloud Hypervisor), orchestrated declaratively by Cluster API provider CAPMVM.
- Copy: the plan-of-idempotent-steps shape for VM mutations (create tap -> prepare rootfs from snapshot manifest -> spawn CH -> verify boot), where each step checks-then-acts so a crashed plan can rerun from the top.
- Avoid: their verified failure mode (issue #326): flintlock marked a VM CREATED "beyond seeing that the call to FC api succeeds, we do not know the result" - the process "started and died and we dont check." Lesson: status transitions require observed liveness (process alive + heartbeat/API ping), never API-call success alone. The lease heartbeat_at_utc is exactly the right countermeasure - make the reconciler treat "spawn returned Ok" as PENDING until first heartbeat.
- Sources: https://github.com/liquidmetal-dev/flintlock , https://github.com/liquidmetal-dev/flintlock/issues/326 , https://buf.build/weaveworks-liquidmetal/flintlock/raw/58fe9b39fd874ce7abc0773abe71f072/-/types/microvm.proto , https://github.com/liquidmetal-dev/flintlock/tree/main/docs/adr

P11. firecracker-containerd: shim-per-VM, containerd as state store
- Mechanism: control plugin + out-of-process shim per VM (ttrpc) + in-VM agent; VM lifecycle modeled via a dedicated "control" API; "a VM should not be terminated as long as there are some containers running in it (unless it's an impairment event like reboot)." Design docs contain no host-reboot recovery story - VMs are effectively ephemeral; durable truth lives in containerd metadata, and reboot survival is out of scope.
- Who: firecracker-microvm/firecracker-containerd (AWS).
- Copy: the process-supervision split - one lightweight supervisor handle per VM owning its socket/PID, distinct from the fleet reconciler; and the impairment-event rule (host reboot invalidates all runtime state, only durable registry survives).
- Avoid: their ephemerality assumption is the opposite of the persistent-workspace requirement - do not copy their lifecycle model wholesale; the snapshot-manifest restore path is the differentiator.
- Sources: https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker-containerd/blob/main/docs/architecture.md , https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker-containerd/blob/main/docs/design-approaches.md , https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker-containerd/blob/main/docs/shim-design.md

P12. Weave Ignite (archived) - cautionary tale, not a pattern source
- Mechanism: GitOps-declarative Firecracker VMs with container UX; repo archived Dec 7, 2023, README redirects to Flintlock; Weaveworks shut down Feb 5, 2024 after an M&A fell through - archival was maintainership/business death, not a technical repudiation of declarative VM management.
- Copy heuristic: the reason it is safe to ignore: it validates the hard rule - Ignite depended on Docker/containerd/CNI plumbing and died with its vendor; a product-native Rust implementation has no such dependency to be orphaned by.
- Sources: https://github.com/weaveworks/ignite , https://thenewstack.io/end-of-an-era-weaveworks-closes-shop-amid-cloud-native-turbulence/ , https://www.theregister.com/2024/02/06/weaveworks_folds/

P13. Cloud Hypervisor snapshot/restore/live-upgrade discipline
- Mechanism: pause -> ch-remote snapshot file://... -> restore creates "the exact same virtual machine... restored in a paused state" -> explicit resume. v53 adds an offloaded snapshot/restore daemon (external process does the heavy lifting) and background prefault after userfaultfd restore. Live "upgrade" = snapshot on old VMM binary, restore on new one.
- Who: cloud-hypervisor project (Rust; rust-vmm-based).
- Copy: the explicit paused-intermediate-state - model PAUSED_FOR_SNAPSHOT / RESTORED_PAUSED as first-class reconciler states so a crash mid-snapshot leaves an unambiguous resumable state; use snapshot-restore as the VMM-binary-upgrade path.
- Avoid: treating snapshot as instantaneous/atomic in the state machine.
- Sources: https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/blob/main/docs/snapshot_restore.md , https://www.cloudhypervisor.org/blog/cloud-hypervisor-v53.0-released/
- Note: rust-vmm crates are VMM building blocks (vm-memory, kvm-ioctls...), not fleet managers - no reconciliation patterns to copy there beyond what the existing CH adapter already embodies. (UNVERIFIED beyond general project scope; not deep-dived.)

## Section 4 - Concurrency correctness

P14. Single-writer via Postgres, not distributed leases
- Mechanism: three field options: (a) K8s Lease-based leader election (client-go: LeaseDuration ~60s / RenewDeadline ~15s / RetryPeriod ~5s); (b) Postgres session advisory lock as leader election - winner holds pg_advisory_lock, crash drops the session, next instance takes over; (c) per-item claims with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Oxide RFD 373 warns time-based distributed leases "implicitly assume something about the liveness of that system" (citing Kleppmann) and prefers DB-backed exclusion only when unavoidable.
- Who: K8s controllers (a); Postgres-backed schedulers/cron (b, c); Oxide Nexus (c-equivalent on CockroachDB).
- Copy: for a single-host local-first product: one reconciler process holding a session-level advisory lock as the crown ("only one reconciler daemon"), plus per-worktree transaction-scoped claims (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on the binding row) inside each reconcile pass. The existing restart_generation fencing then rejects stale writers at the data layer even if locking fails - belt and suspenders, matching RFD 373's generation-number guidance ("unique, monotonically increasing integers"; full-state updates "repair any previous corruption").
- Avoid: wall-clock lease comparisons as the ONLY exclusion; session advisory locks without a fencing token (leaked lock != safe writer).
- Sources: https://kerkour.com/postgresql-leader-election-advisory-lock , https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373 , https://www.postgresscripts.com/post/postgresql-advisory-locks-with-pg-advisory-lock/ , https://sklar.rocks/kubernetes-leader-election/

P15. Per-item exponential backoff + global token bucket
- Mechanism: controller-runtime's default rate limiter = per-item exponential backoff (base ~5ms, cap ~1000s) combined with a global token bucket (~10 QPS, burst ~100); per-item means one broken object backs off alone; backoff resets on success. Jitter prevents thundering herd when many items fail together.
- Who: Go controller-runtime / client-go workqueue; kube-rs error_policy gives the hook to implement the same.
- Copy: store consecutive_failures + next_attempt_at_utc per binding; backoff = min(base * 2^n, cap) with full jitter; a global semaphore caps concurrent VM operations (snapshot restores are IO-heavy - startup stampede control).
- Avoid: global-only backoff (one poison VM stalls the fleet) and unjittered synchronized retries after reconciler restart.
- Sources: https://danielmangum.com/posts/controller-runtime-client-go-rate-limiting/ , https://stuartleeks.com/posts/error-back-off-with-controller-runtime/ , https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/issues/631

P16. Poison objects: quarantine, not dead-letter deletion
- Mechanism: K8s has no true dead-letter queue - the max-backoff cap IS the poison handling (retry forever, slowly). Field guidance adds circuit breakers: "if something fails repeatedly, stop retrying and alert operators." Oxide RPWs likewise "retry indefinitely until convergence" but demand per-target stall metrics ("raise alarms if an RPW hasn't been able to propagate to a particular target for longer than we expect").
- Who: controller-runtime (implicit), Oxide RFD 373 (explicit monitoring).
- Copy: after N failures set binding health = QUARANTINED, keep a slow retry (e.g. 15 min), emit an EventLedger alert record, and require operator/agent action to clear. Never auto-delete a workspace binding as "dead-lettering" - these are user worktrees, not disposable jobs.
- Avoid: infinite fast retry (log flood + CPU burn) and silent max-backoff purgatory with no alert surface.
- Sources: https://www.golinuxcloud.com/avoid-kubernetes-operator-reconcile-loop-explosions/ , https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373 , https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-09-reconciliation-loops-exponential-backoff/view

P17. Startup stampede: staggered warm-up
- Mechanism: on controller start, every object triggers at once; mitigations = global rate limiter + jitter (P15) + bounded concurrency. For VM fleets, restore is expensive, so bound parallel restores explicitly.
- Copy: boot sequence = orphan reconciliation (exists) -> enqueue all bindings with jittered initial delays -> Semaphore-bounded restore concurrency (e.g. 2-4 parallel CH restores), priority to leases with recent heartbeats.
- Avoid: restoring all VMs concurrently on boot; also avoid NOT enqueueing everything (silent drift).
- Sources: https://danielmangum.com/posts/controller-runtime-client-go-rate-limiting/ , https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373

## Section 5 - Rust implementation guidance

P18. Task topology: JoinSet/TaskTracker + CancellationToken
- Mechanism: tokio's documented graceful-shutdown triad: "figuring out when to shut down, telling every part of the program to shut down, waiting for them to finish" - CancellationToken (tokio-util) for signal, TaskTracker or JoinSet to await completion; kube-rs mirrors this with .graceful_shutdown_on() letting in-flight reconciles finish.
- Who: tokio official topic docs; kube-rs; tokio-graceful-shutdown crate for subsystem trees.
- Copy: one long-lived controller task per concern (listener, ticker, dispatcher) + a JoinSet of in-flight per-worktree reconciles; on shutdown, cancel the TRIGGER sources but let running reconciles complete (VM ops mid-flight should finish, not be dropped).
- Avoid: task::abort() on reconciles that are mid-VM-mutation.
- Sources: https://tokio.rs/tokio/topics/shutdown , https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/task/task_tracker/struct.TaskTracker.html , https://crates.io/crates/tokio-graceful-shutdown

P19. Cancellation-safety discipline around side-effectful VM ops
- Mechanism: select! drops losing futures; "if those futures own some form of state, your future is not cancellation safe." Oxide RFD 400 and sunshowers' analysis: make code cancel-safe where reasonable and clearly mark the rest as not cancel-safe; keep state in the channel/target, not the future (recv() pattern).
- Who: Oxide (RFD 400), tokio ecosystem practice.
- Copy: never put a CH-adapter mutation (spawn/snapshot/kill) inside a select! arm that can lose. Shape: select! only over pure waits (watch channel, tick, token); once triggered, run the reconcile body as a spawned task polled to completion. Journal intent to Postgres (EventLedger INTENT_* record) BEFORE the side effect so a crash/cancel mid-operation is repairable by the next level-triggered pass - the same trick as P2's check-every-property.
- Avoid: holding &mut VM handles across await points inside cancellable futures; assuming Drop runs cleanup for async ops.
- Sources: https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0400 , https://sunshowers.io/posts/cancelling-async-rust/ , https://developerlife.com/2024/07/10/rust-async-cancellation-safety-tokio/

P20. State machines: hand-rolled enums, transitions persisted
- Mechanism: field consensus (Polar Signals, S2, RisingWave DST writing): model core components as explicit single-threaded state machines with typed transitions rather than reaching for framework crates; the enum lives in Rust, the CURRENT STATE lives in Postgres.
- Who: Polar Signals, S2.dev, Oxide (statically defined background tasks, RFD 373).
- Copy: hand-rolled enum VmLifecycle { Pending, Restoring, RestoredPaused, Running, PausedForSnapshot, Quarantined, TearingDown, Gone } with a single fn step(observed, desired) -> Plan pure function; persist transitions with generation fencing. No state-machine crate dependency needed at this size.
- Avoid: statechart frameworks that hide transitions from the diffing logic. UNVERIFIED: specific state-machine crates (e.g. statig) not benchmarked - not needed given the hand-rolled recommendation.
- Sources: https://www.polarsignals.com/blog/posts/2025/07/08/dst-rust , https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0373

P21. Testing: proptest-state-machine for logic, madsim-style determinism for the loop
- Mechanism: proptest-state-machine checks a system under test against an abstract reference state machine, shrinking to a minimal failing transition sequence, with a recorded seed for deterministic replay. madsim provides a tokio-compatible deterministic runtime with failure injection ("deterministically reproduce until fixed"). The pure-step() design in P20 is what makes the cheap option (proptest over the pure function + a fake CH adapter + fake clock) sufficient without swapping runtimes.
- Who: madsim: RisingWave et al.; proptest-state-machine: Heliax/Anoma-lineage, general ecosystem; DST pattern: S2, Polar Signals, FOSDEM 2026 talk.
- Copy: (1) property-test step() against a reference model: "after any sequence of crashes/restarts/stale generations, one more converged pass reaches desired state and never double-spawns a VM for one worktree"; (2) integration harness with trait-mocked CH adapter injecting spawn-succeeds-then-process-dies (the flintlock #326 scenario) as a named regression case.
- Avoid: adopting madsim wholesale if it forces runtime abstraction through the whole product; only the reconciler crate needs determinism.
- Sources: https://docs.rs/proptest-state-machine , https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/proptest/state-machine.html , https://github.com/madsim-rs/madsim , https://s2.dev/blog/dst , https://fosdem.org/2026/schedule/event/GNTZDT-rust-deterministic-simulation-testing/

## Recommended architecture sketch (10 lines)

1. One reconciler daemon per host, crowned via Postgres session advisory lock; all writes additionally fenced by the existing restart_generation columns (lock = liveness, fence = safety).
2. Triggers: Postgres LISTEN on binding/lease writes + full-fleet resync tick (60-300s) + boot-time orphan pass - all three collapse into per-worktree tokio::sync::watch activation flags (Oxide RPW pattern); triggers carry no payload.
3. A dispatcher drains activated worktrees through SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claims into a JoinSet of reconcile tasks, bounded by a global Semaphore (2-4 concurrent CH restores) with full-jitter delays to kill startup stampede.
4. Each reconcile is level-triggered: fresh-read binding + lease + observed VM state (process alive AND heartbeat fresh - never trust spawn-Ok, per flintlock #326), then a pure step(observed, desired) -> Plan over a hand-rolled lifecycle enum.
5. Plans are ordered idempotent check-then-act steps (flintlock pattern); every side-effectful step journals an intent record to the EventLedger before acting, so any crash is repaired by the next pass.
6. Teardown uses a Postgres-native finalizer: tombstone column instead of row delete; reconciler runs cleanup (kill VM, release lease, archive snapshot manifest) to completion before the row is archived; stuck tombstones alert.
7. Errors route through one error_policy: per-worktree exponential backoff (consecutive_failures, next_attempt_at_utc, cap ~15 min, reset on success); after N failures -> QUARANTINED health state with slow retry + EventLedger alert, never auto-delete.
8. select! arms contain only pure waits (watch/tick/cancel-token); reconcile bodies run as spawned tasks polled to completion; shutdown = CancellationToken cancels triggers, JoinSet drains in-flight VM operations.
9. Snapshot/restore models CH's paused intermediate states (RestoredPaused, PausedForSnapshot) as first-class enum states, doubling as the VMM live-upgrade path.
10. Tests: proptest-state-machine over step() with a reference model (convergence + no-double-spawn invariants) plus a trait-mocked CH adapter harness with named crash-injection regressions; no K8s, Docker, Nomad, or madsim runtime dependency anywhere in the product.

KEY FINDING: Oxide's RFD 373 (Reliable Persistent Workflows) is a near-exact prior art for Handshake's design - a production Rust control plane doing level-triggered reconciliation over a SQL store with generation numbers and no Kubernetes - and its warnings (queues cause thundering herds; distributed leases are unsafe without fencing; full-state updates over deltas because they "repair any previous corruption") map one-to-one onto the primitives Handshake already has.
catalogs.durable_volumes_and_handoff:
# Pattern Catalog: Durable Workspace Storage + Product Handoff for microVM Agent Workspaces

Anything not pinned to a fetched primary source is labeled UNVERIFIED.

## Area 1 - Guest-visible storage options

P1. virtio-fs via virtiofsd (shared host directory)
- Mechanism: vhost-user-fs device; a separate host daemon (virtiofsd, Rust, gitlab.com/virtio-fs/virtiofsd) serves FUSE over virtio; requires --memory shared=on in Cloud Hypervisor; CH default cache=never.
- Who uses it: Kata Containers, libvirt/QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor.
- Copy heuristic: use it only for the SOURCE TREE (worktree bind), where the host is the writer of record and durability lives on the host FS anyway. It is a managed subprocess - fits the "internalize as managed subprocess" rule.
- Avoid: using virtio-fs as the durability layer for work products. It is a per-VM daemon with no reconnect story: Kata issue #2315 documents that if virtiofsd dies, the guest mount hangs and the sandbox is torn down; Kata #2797 catalogs a family of virtiofsd crash modes. VMM crash = daemon orphaned; daemon crash = guest FS dead. Data already fsync'd by virtiofsd to the host FS survives, but in-flight guest state does not, and the guest cannot recover the mount.
- Sources: https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/blob/main/docs/fs.md , https://gitlab.com/virtio-fs/virtiofsd , https://virtio-fs.gitlab.io/design.html , https://github.com/kata-containers/runtime/issues/2315 , https://github.com/kata-containers/runtime/issues/2797

P2. virtio-blk with raw/qcow2 image files
- Mechanism: block device backed by a host file; Cloud Hypervisor has Rust-native qcow2 support including backing files (since v34) and an io_uring async qcow2 backend (v51 QcowDiskAsync); also raw and VHDX. In-VMM, no sidecar daemon.
- Who uses it: Firecracker (virtio-blk only - deliberately no virtio-fs), Cloud Hypervisor, Kata (virtio-blk preferred over 9pfs for data volumes).
- Copy heuristic: this is the Docker-volume analog: one qcow2/raw file per named volume on host disk = durable unit whose lifetime is decoupled from the VM. VMM crash loses only unflushed writes; the file persists. This is the right home for durable workspace volumes.
- Avoid: assuming guest sync() reaches the host platter by default - see P8. Avoid qcow2 for the hot write path without qemu-img-check-style repair (see P9); raw files have no metadata to corrupt.
- Sources: https://www.phoronix.com/news/Cloud-Hypervisor-34 , https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/releases/tag/v51.0 , https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor , https://dev.to/gansvv/storage-for-kata-containers-9pfs-vs-virtio-blk-f6n

P3. 9p
- Mechanism: network filesystem protocol tunneled over virtio.
- Who uses it: legacy QEMU virtfs; WSL2's /mnt/c drvfs mounts (UNVERIFIED here, widely documented).
- Copy heuristic: none - virtio-fs supersedes it on performance and POSIX compliance (that was virtio-fs's design rationale).
- Avoid: everything; also avoid putting worktrees on /mnt/c inside WSL2 - 9p/NTFS path is the slow path.
- Sources: https://www.phoronix.com/news/Linux-5.4-VirtIO-FS , https://virtio-fs.gitlab.io/

WSL2 caveats: KVM inside WSL2 requires nestedVirtualization=true (Windows 11) and is a recurring breakage surface (WSL #11216, WSL #40736). Treat "host crash" as including WSL utility-VM teardown (wsl --shutdown, Windows update): durable volume files must live on the WSL ext4 VHDX and be fsync'd; there is a second flush layer (WSL VHDX -> NTFS) not under our control - UNVERIFIED depth, plan a snapshot-export to Windows-side storage for backups.
- Sources: https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/11216 , https://github.com/microsoft/wsl/issues/40736

## Area 2 - Copy-on-write layering

P4. qcow2 backing chains (base image + per-workspace delta)
- Mechanism: read-only base qcow2; each workspace disk is a new qcow2 whose backing file points at the base; writes go to the delta only. CH supports this natively in Rust - no QEMU dependency.
- Who uses it: QEMU/libvirt external snapshots everywhere; CH since v34.
- Copy heuristic: one shared read-only rootfs base per toolchain version + one small delta per workspace = instant provisioning, cheap disk. Registry row (Postgres) records base-digest -> delta-file -> workspace binding.
- Avoid: deep chains (each hop adds lookup cost and one more corruptible metadata file); never write to a base that has children (QEMU docs: modifying the backing file invalidates all overlays).
- Sources: https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/system/qemu-block-drivers.html , https://www.phoronix.com/news/Cloud-Hypervisor-34

P5. overlayfs inside the guest
- Mechanism: guest mounts read-only base (virtio-blk or virtio-pmem) as lowerdir + writable upperdir on the durable volume; file-level copy-up.
- Who uses it: Docker overlay2 (image layers = lowerdirs, container layer = upperdir, <=128 layers), Kata, most container runtimes.
- Copy heuristic: use it in-guest to compose "shared toolchain + workspace scratch" without any host-side CoW format at all; keeps the host artifact a plain raw ext4 image.
- Avoid: write-heavy data in the upper layer of large files (copy-up copies whole files - Docker docs explicitly say use volumes for write-heavy paths).
- Sources: https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/ , https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/overlayfs.html (standard kernel doc, not fetched)

P6. device-mapper thin provisioning (dm-thin)
- Mechanism: kernel block-level CoW pool; snapshots via dmsetup messages; snapshot-of-snapshot supported.
- Who uses it: LVM thin, old Docker devicemapper driver.
- Copy heuristic: only if qcow2 is outgrown (hundreds of workspaces, block-level dedup pressure).
- Avoid: for Handshake now - kernel doc itself warns snapshot-of-active-origin without suspend corrupts and "is NOT enforced"; root privileges + host kernel state = poor fit for a local-first product on WSL2.
- Source: https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/device-mapper/thin-provisioning.html

P7. Docker's reference model (the mental model to mirror)
- Read-only image layers + one writable container layer (discarded with container) + named volumes (survive container removal, live in a daemon-managed directory, addressed by name in a registry). Rust-native equivalent: base rootfs image (content-addressed, read-only) + per-workspace qcow2 delta (disposable) + named durable volume (raw/qcow2 file, Postgres-registered, lifetime independent of VM).
- Source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/

## Area 3 - Crash consistency

P8. Honor guest flush with host fsync (VIRTIO_BLK_F_FLUSH -> fsync)
- Mechanism: guest fsync emits VIRTIO_BLK_T_FLUSH; the VMM must fsync the backing file. Firecracker shipped for years acknowledging-and-ignoring flush (issue #2172: guest "synced" data lived only in host page cache); PR #2447 added cache_type: Unsafe (ignore flush, still default) vs Writethrough (fsync on flush + fsync on device drop).
- Who uses it: Firecracker (opt-in), QEMU (cache=writeback honors flush by default).
- Copy heuristic: for durable volumes, run the flush-honoring mode and have the guest agent fsync at commit points (end of MT, before export). Verify Cloud Hypervisor's flush path once in our own harness - CH-specific flush semantics: UNVERIFIED here (class-level behavior verified via Firecracker).
- Avoid: "Unsafe"-cache-mode defaults for anything promised to survive a kill; also avoid fsync-per-write (Firecracker's own measurements in #2172 show 4x throughput delta - flush at commit points, not continuously).
- Sources: https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker/issues/2172 , https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker/pull/2447

P9. qcow2 corruption modes + offline check/repair
- Mechanism: qcow2 keeps refcounts/L1/L2 metadata; crash mid-write can leak clusters (harmless) or corrupt refcounts/offsets (real damage); qemu-img check -r leaks is zero-risk, -r all rewrites metadata; images self-mark corrupt and refuse writes.
- Copy heuristic: on workspace reattach after unclean shutdown, run a check gate before boot (CH's Rust qcow2 means internalizing an equivalent checker, or keep deltas disposable so "repair" = discard delta, keep named volume raw).
- Avoid: putting the named durable volume itself on qcow2 without a checker - use raw for the volume, qcow2 only for the disposable delta.
- Sources: https://rlife.in/posts/qcow2-free-clusters-crash-fix/ , https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/2909

P10. Snapshot-before-teardown
- Mechanism: CH vm.snapshot writes memory-ranges (sparse via SEEK_DATA/SEEK_HOLE) + human-readable state.json; restore resumes paused.
- Copy heuristic: on graceful workspace close: guest-agent fsync -> VM pause -> snapshot -> registry manifest row -> teardown. Crash path then only ever loses post-last-flush writes on the volume, never the volume.
- Avoid: treating VM snapshots as the durability mechanism for DATA - they are resume/latency tools; disk durability comes from P8.
- Source: https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/blob/main/docs/snapshot_restore.md

## Area 4 - Content-addressed export + promotion

P11. OCI descriptor/manifest as format heuristic
- Mechanism: everything is a blob addressed by digest; a manifest is a typed JSON listing descriptors {mediaType, digest, size}; the manifest's own digest names the bundle; the whole thing is a Merkle DAG. OCI artifact spec generalizes this beyond images (SBOMs, signatures, attestations).
- Copy heuristic: define a Handshake "workspace bundle manifest" (serde JSON): typed entries - patch (git bundle), artifact, test-log - each with sha256 digest + size + mediaType; store manifest digest in the Postgres registry and reference it from EventLedger. No OCI dependency, just the shape.
- Sources: https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/descriptor.md , https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/manifest.md , https://oras.land/docs/concepts/artifact/

P12. CAS on disk, Rust-native
- Mechanism: cacache crate - concurrent content-addressed disk cache, atomic (write-temp-then-rename), integrity-verified on read, "never gives corrupted data"; sccache and Bazel remote caches use the same shape: /cas/<sha256> for blobs + /ac/<action-hash> for pointers (Bazel: action cache maps action hash -> output digests).
- Copy heuristic: bundle store = cacache (or a small internal equivalent) keyed by sha256; the Postgres registry plays Bazel's "action cache" role: run-id -> manifest digest -> blob digests. Dedup across workspaces falls out for free.
- Avoid: mutable named files as the artifact store - names go in Postgres, bytes go in CAS.
- Sources: https://github.com/zkat/cacache-rs , https://bazel.build/remote/caching , https://github.com/buchgr/bazel-remote

P13. Git object model + git bundle / format-patch for the patch payload
- Mechanism: git is itself a sha-addressed CAS (blob/tree/commit DAG); git bundle packs refs+objects into one verifiable file usable with fetch/clone offline; git bundle verify checks prerequisites against the receiving repo - a built-in promotion precondition check. format-patch is the human-reviewable alternative but loses binary fidelity/merge base precision.
- Copy heuristic: export workspace diffs as a git bundle with recorded prerequisite commit (the worktree base SHA); promotion gate runs bundle verify against the authoritative repo before apply. Hash the bundle file into the manifest (P11).
- Sources: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bundle , https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Internals-Git-Objects

P14. in-toto/SLSA-style attestation as heuristic
- Mechanism: attestation = {subject: [{name, digest}], predicateType, predicate}; SLSA provenance predicate = "builder X produced subjects from materials Y by recipe Z", signed (DSSE).
- Copy heuristic: each bundle gets a provenance record - subjects = bundle blob digests; predicate = {workspace-id, VM-id, base-image digest, worktree base SHA, MT-id, tool versions}; write it as an EventLedger event (the ledger's append-only signature substitutes for DSSE in a local-first single-operator product). Validation gates check subject digests before promotion.
- Sources: https://slsa.dev/spec/v0.1/provenance , https://slsa.dev/blog/2023/05/in-toto-and-slsa

## Area 5 - GC that can never eat un-promoted work

P15. Mark-and-sweep needs the world stopped - do not copy it
- Docker distribution GC is explicitly stop-the-world: mark reachable digests from manifests, sweep the rest; docs warn concurrent uploads during GC can delete layers of in-flight images. That race is the canonical "GC ate my data" mode. No single famous public postmortem found (UNVERIFIED that one exists); the lesson is instead encoded in the designs below.
- Source: https://docker-docs.uclv.cu/registry/garbage-collection/

P16. Leases / GC fencing (containerd)
- Mechanism: containerd GCs any unreferenced resource; clients take a LEASE covering everything they are mid-creating; leased content is exempt until lease release/expiry; labels add expiry and keep-alive hints.
- Copy heuristic: this is the fence: an open workspace or in-flight export holds a Postgres lease row over its volume + pending blobs; the GC query joins against leases and can structurally never select leased objects. Lease expiry only via explicit close or operator action - never wall-clock alone for un-promoted work.
- Source: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/main/docs/garbage-collection.md

P17. Online GC with review queues + grace period (GitLab registry)
- Mechanism: GitLab replaced offline mark-sweep with online GC over a Postgres-backed metadata DB: deletions enqueue into review queues; workers re-verify reachability at review time; unreferenced blobs get a 24h grace period before deletion.
- Copy heuristic: identical stack to Handshake (Postgres registry as truth). GC = SQL reachability over {EventLedger promotions UNION registry bindings UNION leases}; candidates enter a review queue with grace period; second reachability check at delete time inside one transaction with the writer-visible lease table.
- Sources: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/5024 , https://docs.gitlab.com/administration/packages/container_registry/ , https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/container-registry/-/issues/199

P18. Refcounting vs mark-and-sweep; quotas
- Copy heuristic: with an authoritative Postgres graph, do periodic mark-and-sweep as SQL (robust to crash - recomputed each run) rather than maintaining live refcounts (drift under crashes is exactly what refcounts are bad at). Enforce per-workspace byte quotas as PROMOTION PRESSURE (block new writes / force export) - never as auto-delete of un-promoted volumes; Kubernetes image-GC pinning is the field precedent for "some objects are never evictable". Hard invariant: only objects whose digests appear in a promoted or expired-and-operator-acknowledged state are sweepable; un-promoted work is structurally unreachable to the sweeper.
- Sources: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/main/docs/garbage-collection.md , https://thelinuxnotes.com/pinning-container-images-in-kubernetes-to-prevent-garbage-collection/

## Recommended architecture sketch (10 lines)

1. Base rootfs = content-addressed read-only image (raw or qcow2), digest-registered in Postgres; one per toolchain version.
2. Per-workspace boot disk = qcow2 delta with backing=base (CH-native Rust qcow2); disposable - corruption remedy is "discard delta, re-derive".
3. Named durable volume = raw ext4 image file per workspace, attached virtio-blk, registered worktree->VM->volume in the existing Postgres binding registry; source worktree stays virtio-fs read-mostly.
4. VMM block device runs flush-honoring mode; guest agent fsyncs the volume at MT-commit points and before any export; verify CH flush path once in harness (UNVERIFIED until then).
5. Graceful close: fsync -> pause -> CH snapshot -> manifest row; unclean death: volume file survives, delta is checked-or-discarded on reattach.
6. Export: guest agent writes git bundle (with recorded prerequisite base SHA) + artifacts + test logs into an outbox dir on the volume; host packs them into a typed manifest (OCI-descriptor shape: mediaType+sha256+size per entry).
7. Blobs land in a host-side CAS (cacache-style, temp+rename atomic); manifest digest + SLSA-style provenance record (workspace-id, VM-id, base digest, base SHA, MT-id) are appended to EventLedger.
8. Promotion gate: re-hash blobs against manifest, git bundle verify against the authoritative repo, run validation checks; only a passing gate appends the PROMOTED event that makes digests reachable from authority state.
9. GC: Postgres lease rows fence open workspaces and in-flight exports (containerd pattern); periodic SQL mark-and-sweep over EventLedger+registry+leases, GitLab-style review queue + grace period, delete re-verified in the same transaction.
10. Invariant: un-promoted volumes and bundles are lease-held and thus structurally invisible to the sweeper; quota pressure forces export/promotion, never deletion.

KEY RISK: virtiofsd is a per-VM sidecar with crash modes that hang the guest mount (Kata evidence) - keep it for the worktree only, and ensure nothing durability-critical is writable solely through it.
